doc.title: Sheryl Bailey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 24, 2023

title: Building a vocabulary of licks and applying them across chords
summary: She wrote licks in the key found, then applied them to other chords, and turned Clifford Brown's sequences into etudes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Oh I love it. No I just love it because I use that word magic a lot and you just put it in a wonderful context. When you were first on that path of learning/creating your own diary of licks and so forth, were you mostly playing in one key?

I’d write them in the key that I found them, I think, at the time. I’d be interesting if I ever could find that book, wherever it would be. I’d kind of write them in the key that I found them in and then I’d try to work them in to different things. But the thing that’s fascinating about that is that you’re developing your language, you’re developing your vocabulary, but then as you start to understand harmony it starts to expand because you

see that something that you could play on a major seven chord you can also play on a minor seven chord and you can also play on a sus chord. So then it was like all these other applications outside of the thing. It was like this is the thing but now I found — as I understood harmony more I could apply it to more things. And then also the other thing that also would just spin me out — for instance, Clifford Brown to me I think is the most impeccable, perfect soloist. Sound, everything. And he could just play a phrase and the idea, the shape of the phrase, if it was a sequence, would fascinate me so much that you could take for instance some kind of sequence that he would play and just start to play through it diatonically and turn them into etudes. So then you’re starting to generate your language based on the tradition. And it takes time, all this stuff takes a lot of time and study and, but you know it is fascinating. So you have the actual source, the original source, then the applications of it, and then the stuff that you derive from — hey look at that cool shape. What can I do with that? Or maybe I could put it in a minor key. If it’s a major key shape maybe I’ll put it in harmonic minor or I’ll put it in a symmetrical scale. And then all of a sudden these ideas just blossom into possibilities.
